'''Mary Louise Spaeth''' (born 1940) is an American physicist and innovator who is one of the inventors of the [[Dye laser|tunable dye laser]]. Spaeth was the Chief Technology Officer at the start of the [[National Ignition Facility]]. She was inducted into the [[Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory]] Entrepreneurs’  Hall of Fame in 2022. 

== Early life and education ==
Spaeth studied physics and mathematics at [[Valparaiso University]]. She moved to [[Wayne State University]] for graduate studies, and graduated in 1962.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Mary Spaeth {{!}} Innovation and Partnerships Office |url=https://ipo.llnl.gov/success/hall-of-fame/mary-spaeth |access-date=2024-10-01 |website=ipo.llnl.gov}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=SPIE Laser Damage Special Event Sunday Tutorial: The NIF Laser Ignition Driver |url=https://spie.org/laser-damage/event/sunday-tutorial-the-nif-laser-ignition-driver/2689674#_=_ |access-date=2024-10-01 |website=spie.org |language=en}}</ref>

== Research and career ==
Spaeth started her career at [[Hughes Aircraft Company]], where she became interested in laser physics.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=One current, two former Lab scientists inducted into LLNL's Entrepreneurs' Hall of Fame {{!}} Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory |url=https://www.llnl.gov/article/48561/one-current-two-former-lab-scientists-inducted-llnls-entrepreneurs-hall-fame |access-date=2024-10-01 |website=www.llnl.gov |language=en}}</ref> She became frustrated by the fact that lasers emit monochromatic laser light, which meant they could not be tuned for specific functions. [[Peter Sorokin]] at [[IBM]] demonstrated that organic dyes could make appropriate absorbers for [[Q-switching]] ruby lasers, and went on to investigate its fluorescence. At the time, Spaeth had been reading papers about the dyes used for the development of photographs.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last=Hecht |first=Jeff |date=2023 |title=Discovery of the Tunable Dye Laser |url=https://opticaorgdev.blob.core.windows.net/$web/optica/media/osa.history/century_of_optics/1960-1974/94.pdf}}</ref> She studied the molecular energy transfer processes involved with photographic development. The excited state geometries of these photographic dyes were similar to their ground states, which indicated strong absorption and the potential for population inversion. Spaeth recognised that molecules possessed a high number of rotational states, which would increase their gain bandwidth and could allow for wavelength tuning.<ref name=":2" /> She put the dye molecules in a laser cavity and pumped them with a ruby laser, eventually obtaining an emission wavelength that depended on the cell length and mirror spacing.<ref name=":2" /> By 1966, Spaeth had invented the tunable dye laser.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2024-01-07 |title=MOTHERS OF INVENTIONS |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/1997/03/12/mothers-of-inventions/ccb52eec-5018-4aee-aec5-517c5125cb8d/ |access-date=2024-10-01 |newspaper=Washington Post |language=en-US |issn=0190-8286}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Laser Pioneers |url=https://www.photonics.com/Articles/Laser_Pioneers/a64774 |access-date=2024-10-01 |website=www.photonics.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Hecht |first=Jeff |date=2015-09-16 |title=Photonic Frontiers: Spectrometers and Spectroscopy: Looking Back/Looking Forward: Spectrometers and spectroscopy get faster, better, and cheaper |url=https://www.laserfocusworld.com/test-measurement/spectroscopy/article/16551546/photonic-frontiers-spectrometers-and-spectroscopy-looking-back-looking-forward-spectrometers-and-spectroscopy-get-faster-better-and-cheaper |access-date=2024-10-01 |website=Laser Focus World |language=en}}</ref>

Spaeth was involved with the development of tunable dye lasers, and their exploitation in [[atomic vapor laser isotope separation]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=AVLIS: A Technical and Economic Forecast |url=https://inis.iaea.org/collection/NCLCollectionStore/_Public/17/078/17078031.pdf}}</ref> In 1974, she joined the [[Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory]], where she explored the use of tunable dye lasers for uranium enrichment. Her work was adopted by the United States Enrichment Corporation (which became [[Centrus Energy]]).<ref name=":0" /> She was made [[Chief Technologist|Chief Technology Officer]] at the [[National Ignition Facility]] (NIF).{{when?|date=October 2024}} Spaeth was Lead Systems Engineer during the construction of NIF, which made use of innovations in precision, accuracy and optical components. Spaeth ensured the commissioning, installation and acceptance of the high energy laser systems.<ref name=":0" /> Her innovations led to the creation of the NIF laser ignition driver.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Optica Laser Congress plenary speaker explore the past, present and future of laser technology and its applications. {{!}} Optica |url=https://www.optica.org/about/newsroom/news_releases/2023/september/optica_laser_congress_plenary_speakers_explore_the_past_present_and_future_of_laser_technology_and/ |access-date=2024-10-01 |website=www.optica.org}}</ref> 

Spaeth was inducted into the [[Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory]] Entrepreneurs’  Hall of Fame in 2022.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" />
